source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: GPT-3 (text-davinci-003) matched or beat UCLA undergraduates on a new text-based Raven-style Digit Matrices task, zero-shot. Its pattern of difficulty across problem types resembled humans.
numbers: Digit Matrices: human N=40. Generative: GPT-3 vs human odds ratio 1.88 (p=0.005, CI 1.21-2.91). Multiple choice: OR 6.27 (p=2.3e-8). Pattern correlation across 32 subtypes r=0.39 (p=0.027). Best human got every item right.
limits: Authors admit some letter-string material may be on the web. Digit Matrices built to be novel. Zero-shot means no scaffold, so it says little about mapping choice.
agent_relevance: Base models already do relational mapping on clean, small problems. A scaffold need not teach basic mapping; it should guard the failure cases below.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: On four-term verbal analogies GPT-3 did as well as or better than humans on three datasets and slightly worse on one.
numbers: Humans: UCLA VAT N=57; Sternberg and Nigro N=20; Jones et al. N=241 (US MTurk). SAT set of 374 problems, 5 choices, chance 20%: GPT-3 above the estimated high-school SAT average. Jones et al. set: GPT-3 numerically weaker, same range.
limits: Per-dataset accuracies are in figures, not in text; exact percentages not read. Datasets may sit in training data (authors found no memorisation by A:B-only prompts).
agent_relevance: Simple relation matching is cheap for LLMs. The hard part is choosing among rival mappings when surface and structure disagree (see c03, c08, c10).

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: Story analogies (Gentner et al. 1993 materials): GPT-3 did worse than college students, and was reliable only for near (same-entity) analogies, not far ones. GPT-4 was far better.
numbers: GPT-3 vs humans (N=54): OR 0.37 (p=0.0003, CI 0.21-0.63). 15 of 54 students picked the analogous story on every trial. GPT-4, 72 problems: near analogy almost perfect; far analogy above chance, two-sided binomial p=0.0039.
limits: GPT-4 test was run through the chat interface on 72 items only. Forced choice had three options (A, B, both equal); conservative chance set at 50%.
agent_relevance: Direct test of the multiconstraint tension: when entity similarity and causal structure compete, small models follow entity similarity. Use a stronger model for mapping judgment, or make the structure check a separate step.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: Analogical problem solving (Gick and Holyoak radiation problem). GPT-3 used the general/fortress story only when it was the sole source. With distractor stories it lost the solution until told to consider the earlier stories.
numbers: Qualitative single sessions, no counts. Alone: proposed injecting radiation into the tumour. With analogous story: found convergence. With two distractors: failed. With prompt to consider earlier stories: found the general story and convergence. Child gumball task: mapped all correspondences when asked, but could not use them (physical reasoning).
limits: Anecdotal; one transcript per condition. Not a replication with counts.
agent_relevance: Mirrors human retrieval failure. The explicit step 'compare the problem to each candidate source' is needed; the goal constraint has to be applied by prompting, not assumed.

source: Lewis and Mitchell (2024) Using counterfactual tasks to evaluate the generality of analogical reasoning in LLMs
finding: Letter-string analogies with permuted or symbol alphabets: humans stay high, while GPT-3, GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 all drop sharply. A failed generalisation of Webb et al.
numbers: Humans and three GPT models on original and counterfactual alphabets. Human accuracy stays high on all problems. Share of errors using an alternate (valid but less abstract) rule: GPT-3.5 38.59%, GPT-4 22%, GPT-3 5.81%. Human sample N=46 in their data (57 in Webb).
limits: Per-cell accuracies are in figures, not read as numbers. Webb et al. 2024 reply argues the drop is about counting letter positions, not analogy.
agent_relevance: Warns that a mapping that works on familiar content may be retrieval, not structure. Fits G3: test a mapping on a changed (counterfactual) version before trusting it.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2024) Evidence from counterfactual tasks supports emergent analogical reasoning in LLMs
finding: Reply to Hodel and West and to Lewis and Mitchell. GPT-4 with code execution solves the counterfactual letter-string analogies at roughly human level; without code it is much worse. Authors say the failure is in position counting, not in analogy.
numbers: Humans N=99 on shuffled alphabets, interval size 1 or 2. 600 problems per interval size (100 per transformation type). GPT-4 (gpt-4-0125-preview, temperature 0). Code used only to convert letters to indices; the model chose to do this unprompted. Many remaining errors used a valid but less abstract rule.
limits: Authors' own reply, not independent. Letter-string tasks are synthetic and under-determined (several valid answers).
agent_relevance: A tool (code) removes a perception bottleneck so the mapping step can work. Fits the split: program does counting, model does the slot.

source: Hodel and West (2024) Response: Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: Argues the zero-shot claim is unproven because letter-string problems are common online, and GPT-3 fails simple variants (synthetic alphabet plus larger interval) that humans solve.
numbers: GPT-3 comprehension check on counterfactual alphabets: accuracy at least 30% of original level on all but one 'predecessor' case. Human performance stays high on modified problems. Exact numbers are in figures.
limits: Critique paper; GPT-3 only. Webb et al. 2024 answered with GPT-4 plus code.
agent_relevance: Do not read a good score on a public-looking puzzle as evidence of general mapping skill.

source: Sourati, Ilievski, Sommerauer, Jiang (2024) ARN: Analogical Reasoning on Narratives
finding: Benchmark of 1,096 triples built from structure-mapping theory, with near and far analogies and near and far distractors. Models follow surface similarity over system (relational) similarity.
numbers: Humans 96% vs models 57% overall. Near analogies: humans 97.9%, models 75.0% (SBERT 77.9%). Far analogies: humans 94.1%, models 39.6%, below the 50% chance. Partitions: near analogy vs far distractor 76.9%; (near,near) 73.2%; (far,far) 45.3%; far analogy vs near distractor 33.9%. GPT-4 best at 68.1% average; SBERT 42.3% (1% when the far analogy must beat a near distractor).
limits: Proverb-based narratives; distractors built by surface overlap. Authors note the heuristic 'pick the dissimilar story' would win the far-vs-near partition.
agent_relevance: Core evidence for our case: when structure and surface conflict, LLMs weight surface too much, and asking for system mappings in the prompt did not fix it. A multiconstraint step needs an explicit structure score, not only an instruction.

source: Sourati et al. (2024) ARN: demonstration and chain-of-thought study
finding: Solved demonstrations help detection of far analogies but hurt near ones. Far-analogy demonstrations helped slightly more. Step-by-step prompting was also tested.
numbers: Demonstrations in {0,2,4,6}. GPT-3.5 and Llama-2 tested with near-only vs far-only demos; CoT tested with 2, 4, 6 demos split between far and near for Llama-2, GPT-3.5, GPT-4. Gains small and mixed (values in figures, not extracted).
limits: Figure values not extracted. Demos helped one partition at the cost of another.
agent_relevance: Few-shot examples shift the surface/structure balance rather than fix it. Do not add demonstrations as a general cure.

source: Jiayang et al. (2023) StoryAnalogy: story-level analogies from LLMs
finding: 24K story pairs annotated for entity similarity (EntSim) and relation similarity (RelSim), extending structure-mapping to text. Choosing the true analogy (high RelSim, low EntSim) among 4 choices is very hard for LLMs.
numbers: Multiple choice: random 25%, humans 85.7%, ChatGPT about 30%. A fine-tuned FlanT5-xxl generates analogies comparable to zero-shot ChatGPT. Hard negative chosen by high noun similarity (GloVe cosine) with under 50% token overlap.
limits: Stories partly LLM-generated; human annotation drives the labels.
agent_relevance: Gives a measurable two-axis score (entity vs relation). We could score candidate mappings on both axes and prefer high relation, low surface when the goal is transfer.

source: Musker, Duchnowski, Millière, Pavlick (2025) Semantic structure-mapping in LLM and human analogical reasoning
finding: New tasks map between words and symbol strings, needing re-representation of semantic content. GPT-4, Claude 3 and Llama-405B matched humans in many conditions but were more affected by presentation order and by irrelevant semantic distractors.
numbers: Study 1: LLMs sensitive to order and weak with a distractor row. Study 2: best model matched humans in all conditions and beat them in compositional variants where humans were worst. About a fifth of human wrong answers copied a right-hand term. Exact accuracies not read from text.
limits: University-student sample; Llama-405B lower. Authors say models give a how-possibly, not how-actually, account of human analogy.
agent_relevance: A distractor with high surface similarity is exactly where mapping selection fails. A scaffold should strip irrelevant semantic cues, or test the mapping with the cue swapped.

source: Stevenson, ter Veen, Choenni, van der Maas, Shutova (2023) Do LLMs solve verbal analogies like children do?
finding: Six Dutch LLMs score near children on A:B::C:? but much of the success comes from association with C. Controlling for association drops each model by 1-2 years of age level.
numbers: 14,006 children aged 7-12 solved 622 Dutch analogies. M-GPT about age 7; GPT-3 and XLM-V slightly above age 11. After controlling for association, 1-2 year drop. GPT-3 follows children's item pattern; XLM-V is flatter.
limits: Dutch language; older models. Association is what an unchecked semantic-similarity constraint produces.
agent_relevance: Shows what happens when the semantic-similarity constraint dominates. A scaffold needs a check that the answer is not just associated with the cue.

source: Opielka, Rosenbusch, Stevenson (2025) Analogical reasoning inside LLMs: concept vectors and the limits of abstraction
finding: Inside Llama-3.1 8B and 70B, concept vectors stay invariant for verbal concepts (antonym, category) but not for abstract 'previous' and 'next', which tie to known lists and surface format.
numbers: 600 ICL prompts. Zero-shot function vectors work much better than concept vectors (about 50% vs 14% for 8B, 58% vs 2% for 70B). 70B scores 98% on previous/next items but 62% on abstract versions. Invariance grows with training examples and plateaus after about 5.
limits: Only Llama 3.1; interpretability on a narrow task family.
agent_relevance: Supports the claim that abstract relational mapping is partly list/format lookup. Gives a mechanism for why counterfactual alphabets break models.

source: Ichien, Stamenkovic, Holyoak (2023) LLM displays emergent ability to interpret novel literary metaphors
finding: GPT-4 interpreted figurative sentences (Fig-QA) at near-human accuracy zero-shot, and gave critic-accepted readings of novel poetic metaphors.
numbers: Fig-QA test set, 1,146 metaphors: humans 94.42%, GPT-3 Davinci zero-shot 68.41%, fine-tuned RoBERTa 90.32% (fine-tuned on 8,016 items), GPT-4 91.27% (3.35% non-answers counted wrong). Reversed metaphors: GPT-4 restored the canonical meaning 56% vs humans 50%.
limits: Metaphor interpretation is related but narrower than mapping. Possible contamination by known metaphors.
agent_relevance: Semantic and pragmatic constraints are well handled by a strong model when the text carries the context. Safe to rely on for single-sentence mappings.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large language models as analogical reasoners (analogical prompting)
finding: Asking the model to recall relevant solved problems before solving (self-generated exemplars) beats 0-shot CoT and often matches or beats few-shot CoT.
numbers: GSM8K (0-shot / 0-shot CoT / 5-shot CoT / self-generated): GPT-3.5-turbo 75.0/75.8/76.7/77.8; text-davinci-003 14.8/50.3/54.0/61.0; PaLM2 60.8/78.2/80.7/81.7. MATH: GPT-3.5 33.0/33.9/34.9/37.3; PaLM2 27.1/29.8/34.3/34.8. Codeforces Acc@1 GPT-4: 16/16/17/17, and 19 with self-generated knowledge plus exemplars. Gains grow with model size; smaller models do better with retrieved exemplars.
limits: Gains are 1-6 points on strong models. No mapping or multi-constraint scoring; no check that recalled problems are structurally relevant.
agent_relevance: The analogy method most widely used in an LLM loop. It does retrieval with no structure or purpose filter, so its gain is small. A multiconstraint filter on the recalled exemplars is the open step.

source: Bhavya, Xiong, Zhai (2022) Analogy generation by prompting large language models: a case study of InstructGPT
finding: Studies InstructGPT generating explanatory analogies for concepts under different prompt styles. Downloaded but not read in detail.
numbers: No figures claimed.
limits: Not read to the level of numbers. Early model.
agent_relevance: Early example of using target concept and purpose in the prompt to steer source choice.

source: Wijesiriwardene et al. (2023) ANALOGICAL: a novel benchmark for long-text analogy evaluation in LLMs
finding: Six-level taxonomy (word, word vs sentence, syntactic, negation, entailment, metaphor). Eight LLMs on thirteen datasets with three distance measures: analogy detection gets harder up the taxonomy.
numbers: 8 LLMs, 13 datasets, 3 distance measures. Per-level accuracies not extracted.
limits: Embedding-space measure, not generation; no agent loop.
agent_relevance: Shows the gradient: the more world and purpose knowledge needed, the worse the model.

source: Wijesiriwardene, Sheth, Shalin, Das (2023) Why do we need neuro-symbolic AI to model pragmatic analogies?
finding: Position paper. Four levels of analogy: lexical, syntactic, semantic, pragmatic. Cites Holyoak and Thagard's semantic and pragmatic constraints and argues LLMs fall off at the pragmatic level, needing knowledge-graph guidance for mapping.
numbers: No new measurements. Cites Holyoak and Thagard 1989, Spellman and Holyoak 1996, Forbus MAC/FAC, Hofstadter Copycat.
limits: Opinion; evidence is the authors' ANALOGICAL results (c17).
agent_relevance: Backs the design idea: put purpose and world knowledge in as an explicit constraint, since text statistics do not supply it.

source: Lu, Ichien, Holyoak (2022) Probabilistic analogical mapping with semantic relation networks (PAM)
finding: A modern multiconstraint model. Bayesian graph matching with soft constraints on concept similarity, relation similarity, structure, and attention-weighted pragmatic focus. Cites the ACME multiconstraint theory as its ancestor.
numbers: Human mapping study N=1,329. Proportion correct humans vs PAM: 0.74 vs 0.83 (Category triplets), 0.79 vs 0.89 (Part-Object-Location). Pragmatic-focus task: correlation .96 with human response proportions over 10 conditions; reproduced the shift of the ambiguous country's mapping when military or economic relations were stressed, and its asymmetry. Variants without node vectors or without relations failed.
limits: Word-embedding relation vectors; small fixed analogs.
agent_relevance: A tested recipe: score a mapping on semantic, relational and goal weights together. Goal weighting changes the answer, as in humans. Template for a scoring step in code.

source: Khojasteh et al. (2026) Enhancing structural mapping with LLM-derived abstractions for analogical reasoning in narratives (YARN)
finding: Pipeline where an LLM splits stories into units and abstracts them, then code does a greedy one-to-one structural mapping with soft constraints. Mapping raw event text with embeddings is below chance; adding abstraction fixes it.
numbers: MCQ (chance 0.25): Qwen raw structural mapping 0.17, best with abstraction 0.46 vs best LLM-only 0.41; Llama 0.16 to 0.45 vs 0.28 LLM-only (+0.17). ARN far analogy: raw 0.24 (Qwen); YARN beats LLM on far (Llama 0.46 vs 0.42) but loses on near (Qwen CoT 0.79 vs YARN 0.69). Evaluative abstraction as a soft constraint lowered ARN near slightly (Qwen 0.67 to 0.63) but helped MCQ.
limits: Small open models, preprint under review. Most far-analogy results are still near chance.
agent_relevance: Closest thing to a working LLM loop with an explicit mapping step. Division of labour fits us: model abstracts, program maps under hard and soft constraints. Soft constraints are not a free win.

source: Shen, Druckmann, Zou (2026) Unlocking LLM creativity in science through analogical reasoning
finding: An agent step extracts objects and relations from a problem, builds analogies to cross-domain problems, and uses the object mappings to transfer solutions. The prompt says map by function, not surface similarity. It raises diversity and novelty.
numbers: Solution diversity (Vendi score) up 90-173%; domain Vendi up 100-115%. Baselines: domain Vendi 2.64 and 2.84, solution Vendi 5.81 and 8.34 over 150 generations per problem. Novel solutions over 50% of the time vs as little as 1.6% for baselines. Structural Depth 7.06-8.60 in all settings; Domain Distance 6.99/6.83/7.53 vs 2.29/3.08/3.37 for the no-domain baseline. 50 problems, 3 LLMs.
limits: Novelty judged by LLMs plus a human pairwise study; mapping accuracy itself not measured. Structural Depth did not differ from baselines.
agent_relevance: A structure-and-purpose mapping step inside an agent with measured gains in diversity. The gain targets mode collapse, not correctness.

source: Donvito and Lieto (2026) Structural ranking of the cognitive plausibility of computational models of analogy and metaphor
finding: Rates SME, CogSketch, METCL and LLMs against structure-mapping constraints (one-to-one, parallel connectivity, systematicity). Argues LLM answers changing under rephrasing and distractors indicate a break in parallel connectivity.
numbers: Binary scoring of each constraint per system; no experiments on LLM accuracy.
limits: Conceptual scoring by the authors; not an empirical LLM test.
agent_relevance: A checklist of mapping constraints that code can verify on a proposed mapping: one-to-one and parallel connectivity.

source: Holyoak and Thagard (1989) Analogical mapping by constraint satisfaction (ACME)
finding: The founding model. Mapping is a constraint-satisfaction network combining structural consistency, semantic similarity and pragmatic importance. Later papers (c19, c18) call it the first instance of multiconstraint theory.
numbers: Not opened this session; no numbers recorded.
limits: Known only through citations in c18, c19 and c22.
agent_relevance: Source of the idea: weight the three constraints and let the best joint mapping win.

source: Spellman and Holyoak (1996) Pragmatics in analogical mapping
finding: Human study showing that processing goals shift which mapping people prefer when structure is ambiguous (Gulf War vs World War II). PAM simulates it.
numbers: Not opened. PAM (c19) reports correlation .96 with the human pattern.
limits: Claim taken from c19 and c18.
agent_relevance: Purpose is a real, measurable constraint on mapping choice.

source: Hummel and Holyoak (1997) LISA; Forbus, Gentner, Law (1995) MAC/FAC
finding: Later symbolic-connectionist (LISA) and retrieval (MAC/FAC) models that add working-memory limits and fast similarity-based retrieval. Cited in c18 and c19.
numbers: Not opened.
limits: Not read.
agent_relevance: MAC/FAC two-stage retrieval (cheap similarity then structural check) is a pattern to copy for choosing sources.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) Prompt-format sensitivity in letter-string analogies
finding: GPT-3 letter-string performance depended on the prompt: it fell with no prompt, or with the problem written as a sentence.
numbers: Formats: 'Let's try to complete the pattern:' with brackets (main), no prompt, sentence format. 300 zero-generalisation problems (50 per transformation type) plus one- and two-generalisation sets. Humans N=57.
limits: Drop sizes are in figures, not read here.
agent_relevance: Format sensitivity means a mapping prompt must be fixed and tested; wording is not neutral.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) Digit Matrices: number of rules and alignment
finding: More distinct rules hurt both humans and GPT-3. Progression rules were harder. Spatial alignment helped logic problems, as the isomorphism is clearer.
numbers: Progression vs no progression: humans OR 0.41 (p=0.0001), GPT-3 OR 0.07 (p=1.9e-5), so GPT-3 suffers more. Problem-type effect on generative accuracy OR 0.5 (p=2e-16).
limits: Synthetic digit grids.
agent_relevance: LLMs, like humans, pay for each extra constraint held at once; split multi-rule mappings into one rule per step.
